explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Verse 3 says, "And on the eighth day the flesh of the boy’s foreskin is to be circumcised." (Leviticus 12:3) One verse, one job, no extra steps. I wish my own recipes were that short.

explanations.answer: He is named by the priest
explanations.explanation: I get why a naming sounds right for a brand new baby, friend. But this verse never mentions a priest or a name. It says, "…the flesh of the boy’s foreskin is to be circumcised." (Leviticus 12:3) Circumcision is what happens on the eighth day.

explanations.answer: He is brought to the altar
explanations.explanation: An altar is a big deal, so I see why it tempts you. But the baby boy isn't brought anywhere in this verse. The text says the flesh of his foreskin "…is to be circumcised." on the eighth day. (Leviticus 12:3)

Oh, that's a sneaky one, baker, because it sounds like a fair deal. But verse 4 says she "…must not touch anything sacred or go into the sanctuary until the days of her purification are complete." (Leviticus 12:4) That's two limits, not one. Skipping the touching doesn't open the door to the sanctuary.

Right, friend. Verse 4 gives her two limits: she "…must not touch anything sacred or go into the sanctuary until the days of her purification are complete." (Leviticus 12:4) So the sanctuary stays off limits for those thirty-three days, touching or not. Both limits end together, when the days are complete.

There it is, baker. Verse 5 says, "Then she must continue in purification from her bleeding for sixty-six days." (Leviticus 12:5) After a son it's thirty-three, and after a daughter it's sixty-six. Double the number, and I almost doubled the dough just checking my math.

Thirty-three is a real number in this passage, friend, but it belongs to the son. Verse 4 gives thirty-three days after a boy. For a girl, verse 5 says "sixty-six days." (Leviticus 12:5) Same kind of purification, bigger number.

Forty feels like a Bible number, I'll give you that. But it isn't in this passage at all, baker. After a daughter, the text says she continues in purification "…for sixty-six days." (Leviticus 12:5) Keep the thirty-three and sixty-six side by side and they'll stick.

That's right, baker. Verse 6 says she brings "…a year-old lamb for a burnt offering…" (Leviticus 12:6) Not a two-year-old, not a baby one, a year-old lamb. If I tried to carry that to the priest with just my mustache, we'd both end up in the dirt.
A goat is a fair guess, friend, because Leviticus has plenty of animals running around. But this verse names a different one. She brings "…a year-old lamb for a burnt offering…" (Leviticus 12:6)

Ram is close, baker, since it's the same woolly neighborhood. But the text doesn't say ram here. Verse 6 says "…a year-old lamb for a burnt offering…" (Leviticus 12:6) A young one, not a full-grown ram.

Yes, baker. Verse 6 says the woman brings "…a young pigeon or a turtledove for a sin offering." (Leviticus 12:6) So the lamb goes with the burnt offering and the bird goes with the sin offering. Two offerings, two different jobs.

I think the lamb is crowding the picture, friend. The lamb is for the burnt offering. For the sin offering, verse 6 says she brings "…a young pigeon or a turtledove…" (Leviticus 12:6) So the statement is true.

That's the word, baker. Verse 7 says the priest will make atonement for her, "and she shall be ceremonially cleansed from her flow of blood." (Leviticus 12:7) The priest presents the offerings, and then she is cleansed.

Excused sounds like getting out of a meeting, friend. But the verse says something stronger. After atonement, "…she shall be ceremonially cleansed from her flow of blood." (Leviticus 12:7) The word is cleansed.
Released has a nice ring to it, baker, like opening the oven door. But that isn't the word in the text. Verse 7 says "…she shall be ceremonially cleansed from her flow of blood." (Leviticus 12:7)

explanations.answer: Two turtledoves or two young pigeons
explanations.explanation: That's right, friend. Verse 8 says, "But if she cannot afford a lamb, she shall bring two turtledoves or two young pigeons, one for a burnt offering and the other for a sin offering." (Leviticus 12:8) The two birds take the place of the lamb and the one bird from verse 6. The LORD made room for a woman with a thin wallet, and this stamper who cost 25 cents says thank you.

explanations.answer: A tenth of an ephah of flour
explanations.explanation: Flour is a baker's friend, so I get the pull. But that's not what this verse says. A woman who can't afford a lamb "…shall bring two turtledoves or two young pigeons…" (Leviticus 12:8) Birds, not flour. My bakery's loss, friend, but the LORD named the offering and it isn't on my shelf.

explanations.answer: A young goat from the flock
explanations.explanation: A goat is a fair guess, baker, but the text doesn't go there. If she cannot afford a lamb, "…she shall bring two turtledoves or two young pigeons…" (Leviticus 12:8) Two birds, and that's the whole list for this verse.

Yes, baker. Look at how verse 8 ends: "Then the priest will make atonement for her, and she will be clean." (Leviticus 12:8) The smaller offering doesn't get a smaller result. One bird for the burnt offering, one for the sin offering, and the priest does the same work of atonement as with the lamb. I think a woman who couldn't afford a lamb would hear that line and let out a big breath. I'd be doing a happy dance on my gold base.

I can see why you'd think a smaller offering gets a smaller result, friend. But verse 8 says otherwise: "Then the priest will make atonement for her, and she will be clean." (Leviticus 12:8) So the statement is true. The priest still makes atonement for her, and she will be clean.
